title: Maine Seal of Climate Literacy
before:
The Maine Seal of Climate Literacy

The Maine Seal of Climate Literacy diploma endorsement prepares and empowers students with environmental literacy, traditional ecological knowledge, climate action, and green workforce skills. The Seal was launched in 2026, structured on the foundation of Colorado's Seal of Climate Literacy program, established in 2024. Join the effort in preparing our future leaders to tackle climate challenges and support Maine communities today! 

How to Earn the Seal

To achieve this diploma endorsement, Maine high school students must meet the following criteria as determined by their local School Administrative Unit (SAU):

1. Any two high school courses with a focus on climate and environmental literacy concepts and standards.

This may include, but is not limited to, earth science, Wabanaki studies, environmental-focused humanities, biology, or environmental studies. At least one course must include strong elements of traditional ecological knowledge. SAUs should work with students to determine what will qualify.

2. Students must complete an experiential project that demonstrates and publicly communicates their understanding of environmental literacy, green career exploration, and/or place-based climate action.

This project can range from a school compost campaign, engagement with local public policy, to data collection with community organizations, to green job exploration, and anything in between. SAUs should work with students to determine what will qualify.

Experiential Projects

The project is an opportunity for students to explore their own passions beyond the classroom. This project should be locally relevant to climate literacy and should have a publicly communicated element. As a result of these projects, students can have a meaningful impact on their communities and develop important career skills.

Examples of projects could include:

  • Starting a schoolwide composting program.
  • An apprenticeship or Extended Learning Opportunity (ELO) with a high-performance carpentry business.
  • An internship measuring aquaculture water quality with a local non-profit organization.
  • Developing an environmental justice social campaign or film for youth supporting Wabanaki Sovereignty.

Example Project

Awarding Process 

The Maine DOE will offer wooden medals and certificates bearing the Seal of Climate Literacy to all the diploma endorsement recipients. SAUs are welcome to host ceremonies to celebrate their Seal recipients.

Resources

The Maine Seal of Climate Literacy Student Guide provides resources for students interested in incorporating the Seal into their schools! There are recommended steps, email samples, flyer templates, and more.

The Maine Seal of Climate Literacy Coordinator Guide provides resources for approving the Seal, supporting students with their classes and projects, awarding the Seal, and more. In the guide, there are recommended steps, examples of classes/projects, and talking points for approving the Seal!

Thank you so much for your help in creating a more climate-literate future!

If you are an educator interested in incorporating more traditional ecological knowledge into your curriculum or courses, here are some resources to get started!

2025-2026 List of Classes

AP Environmental Science, Biology, AP Biology, Honors Biology, AP Human Geography, Early College US History, Earth Science, Honors Earth Science, Honors Earth and Physical Science

2025-2026 Experiential Projects

Student Representative of the Bar Harbor Climate Task Force, Sea Level Rising Public Awareness Campaign, Ocean Acidification Research, Community Science with Mast Landing School, Addressing the Impacts of Fast Fashion, Hemlock Woolly Adelgid (HWA) Monitoring, Green Crab Monitoring, Sustainable Fisheries and Aquaculture, Traditional Ecological Knowledge and Fisheries, North Atlantic Right Whale Conservation, Working Waterfront Access, Clam Recruitment Monitoring, Forest Soil Microbiome Research 

How to Approve the Seal

School Administrative Units (SAUs) are responsible for approving the Seal of Climate Literacy. SAUs may determine which courses, standards, and experiential projects, and which achievable standards within those areas, meet the criteria. The Maine Department of Education will support SAUs in implementing the Seal of Climate Literacy through resources, communications, and the celebration of student achievement. SAUs and their students may partner with community-based non-profit organizations, local businesses, and higher education institutions.

Why the Seal Matters in Maine

Maine is on the front lines of climate change. Students are growing up amid sea level rise, coastal erosion, intensifying storms, drought, wildfire risk, and heat impacts that affect water systems, housing, food security, and cultural resources. At the same time, Maine is investing in a clean energy transition, climate-resilient infrastructure, conservation, sustainable tourism, and local food systems. Climate literacy is essential to preparing students to participate in these sectors and contribute to resilient communities statewide.

notes: 2 section headers — too few for a contents list.

decisions.label: Draw a closing link as the action it is
decisions.why: 1 passage ends with a paragraph holding nothing but a link — the thing the passage was leading up to. Set as running text it looks like any other link in the sentence above it. The site already has one way of drawing an action, so it takes that. The words do not change.

decisions.label: Separate a link from its description
decisions.why: 1 list item opens with a link and then explain it, all at the same weight — so the thing you can click is no easier to find than the sentence about it. The link becomes the item and the explanation sits under it.

decisions.label: Let a colon do its own work
decisions.why: A colon marks the words before it as a term and the words after it as what the term means. 1 link sits immediately in front of a colon, where the chevron lands between the term and the punctuation that belongs to it. No word changes and nothing is removed.

decisions.label: Make a loose address look like an address
decisions.why: 1 email address sits in the body of this page rather than in a contact block, drawn exactly like every other link — so the one that opens a mail window looks the same as the ones that go to web pages. The chip carries the same envelope the banner's contact link uses. The address itself does not change.

decisions.label: Retire the old banner graphic
decisions.why: It repeats the page title in picture form, which the new banner already does in type.
decisions.removes: Climate Education - Seal of Climate Literacy Banner.png

decisions.label: Bring every heading up to h3 or above
decisions.why: 4 headings sat at h4 or deeper inside a card, a callout, a contact block or an accordion panel — components the outline walk leaves alone because they label a thing rather than a section. A reader using a screen reader still hears the level, so a fourth-level title inside a page that only goes to three is announced as belonging to a level that does not exist. Each is styled by its class and its position rather than its number, so nothing changes on screen.
